steps.title: WOMAN READING, 1880–82
steps.text:
Édouard Manet painted this in Paris a year or two before he died in 1883. It is small, 61 by 51 centimetres, oil on canvas.
Parisian cafés were where painters and writers met. Manet and his friends, Degas, Monet, Renoir and the writer Zola among them, kept two tables at the Café de la Nouvelle-Athènes.

steps.title: THE READER
steps.text:
A young woman in a black hat and a heavy coat looks up from what she is reading. Her coat and kid gloves say the weather is cool: she seems to be sitting at an outdoor table.
Her face is a few quick strokes of pink and white. Manet painted fast, and this is one of his most Impressionist pictures.

steps.title: THE MAGAZINE
steps.text: The pale shape on the left is an illustrated paper, clipped to a wooden bar. Cafés kept their newspapers on bars like this so customers could read them at the table.

steps.title: THE CAFÉ TABLE
steps.text: At the bottom left, the edge of a marble tabletop and a glass mug of beer: everything says café.

steps.title: THE GARDEN BEHIND HER
steps.text: But the flowers and leaves behind her are not a real garden. They are one of Manet's own paintings, hung behind his model. The café is a re-creation in his studio.

steps.title: A MOMENT OF MODERN LIFE
steps.text:
Manet wanted to catch the passing moment of city life, the glance up from a page. The loose, light brushwork is how he did it at the end of his career.
The painting is in the Art Institute of Chicago.

steps.title: IN THE CAFÉ, 1882–84
steps.text:
Fernand Lungren, an American, went to Paris in 1882. He took classes for a short time at the Académie Julian, then left to paint the city and its people directly.
This is oil on canvas, about 80 by 105 centimetres.

steps.title: A WOMAN ALONE
steps.text:
A fashionably dressed woman in red sits by herself at a marble table, upright and alert.
A woman alone in a café was new. Café life was opening public places of leisure to women in modern Paris.

steps.title: THE CARAFE
steps.text: On the table, a glass carafe and a tray. Lungren paints glass and marble with hard, clean edges, sharper than the Impressionists around him.

steps.title: GASLIGHT
steps.text: Two kinds of light fill the room: the warm glow of gas lamps and the new, whiter electric light. Lungren was as interested in light as the Impressionists were.

steps.title: THE EMPTY TABLES
steps.text: Behind her the room opens out: round tables, bentwood chairs, a waiter and other customers far off. The emptiness makes her solitude stronger.

steps.title: AFTER PARIS
steps.text:
Lungren went home to America and became best known for paintings of the deserts of the American Southwest.
This picture is in the Art Institute of Chicago.

steps.title: A SUNDAY ON LA GRANDE JATTE — 1884
steps.text:
Georges Seurat worked on this huge canvas, three metres wide, from 1884 to 1886, and added its painted border in 1888–89.
It shows Parisians of every age and kind on a Sunday afternoon on an island in the river Seine.

steps.title: DOTS
steps.text: Come close and everything turns into dots and dashes of colour laid side by side: orange beside blue, red beside green. Your eye mixes them. The method is called pointillism.

steps.title: THE COUPLE AND THE MONKEY
steps.text: On the right, a couple in profile, she with a parasol and a monkey on a leash. Seurat added some figures two years after he began, the monkey among them.

steps.title: IN THE SHADE
steps.text: In the shade at the lower left, a man reclines with a pipe, another sits in a top hat, a woman reads.

steps.title: THE RIVER
steps.text: Behind them the river: sailboats, a rowing boat and, at the far left, a woman fishing.

steps.title: A MODERN FRIEZE
steps.text: Seurat wanted a painting of modern life as calm and still as a frieze on an ancient Greek temple. It was first shown at the last Impressionist exhibition in 1886, and has hung in the Art Institute of Chicago since 1924.

steps.title: PARIS STREET; RAINY DAY, 1877
steps.text:
Gustave Caillebotte's largest and most ambitious painting, more than two by two and a half metres. He showed it at the Impressionists' exhibition of 1877.
It is a busy crossing a short walk from his home in Paris.

steps.title: THE COUPLE
steps.text: A well-dressed couple share an umbrella and walk straight toward us, looking at something outside the picture. The sharp cut at the edges may come from photography, new then.

steps.title: THE RAIN
steps.text: You never see a raindrop. The rain is in the open umbrellas, new retractable ones, and in the shine on the wet cobblestones.

steps.title: THE LAMPPOST
steps.text: A green gas lamppost splits the picture in two, the crowd and the couple on one side, the open square on the other.

steps.title: THE NEW CITY
steps.text: The tall pale buildings are the new Paris, rebuilt with wide straight streets in the decades before. Caillebotte placed every figure carefully to make the city feel busy.

steps.title: A FRIEND OF THE IMPRESSIONISTS
steps.text:
Caillebotte exhibited with the Impressionists and helped pay for their shows. His style is more exact than theirs, but his subject is the same: modern life.
The painting has been in the Art Institute of Chicago since 1964.

steps.title: CAFÉ SINGER, 1879
steps.text:
Edgar Degas loved the café-concerts of Paris: outdoor cafés where singers performed on a lit stage while the audience drank.
This small oil, 54 by 42 centimetres, is one of several pictures he made of the singers.

steps.title: MID-SONG
steps.text: Her mouth is wide open: Degas caught her in the middle of a note. Her face is lit hard from below, by the footlights of the stage.

steps.title: THE BLACK GLOVE
steps.text: Her arm swings up in a long black glove. Café singers sang with big gestures so the back of the crowd could see them. The glove makes the gesture a dark shape against the light.

steps.title: THE RED FLOWER
steps.text: A spot of red at her bodice, a flower or a ribbon, the brightest thing in a picture of dark greens and blacks.

steps.title: THE STAGE
steps.text: Behind her, the painted scenery and the glow of the stage. Degas paints it loosely, so all the attention stays on her.

steps.title: FROM MEMORY
steps.text:
Degas sketched in the cafés and painted later in his studio. He said he wanted to paint people as if seen through a keyhole: caught, not posed.
The painting is in the Art Institute of Chicago.

steps.title: INTERRUPTED READING, c. 1870
steps.text:
Camille Corot was famous for dreamy landscapes. He also painted figures, but almost never showed them.
This is one of his late figure paintings, oil on canvas, 92 by 65 centimetres.

steps.title: THE PAUSE
steps.text: She has stopped reading and leans her head on her hand, lost in thought. Corot paints her looking up from the book, not into it: the mood is quiet and a little sad.

steps.title: THE DETAILS
steps.text: Corot liked small things: the red ribbon in her hair, the delicate earrings, the coral necklace.

steps.title: THE BOOK
steps.text: Down in her lap, the book, her finger still keeping the place.

steps.title: THE SKIRT
steps.text: The skirt is painted in broad, bold strokes. Corot built the body as blocks of form that balance each other, a modern way of painting an old subject.

steps.title: AN ITALIAN COSTUME
steps.text:
Corot spent years in Italy and loved everything Italian; he often dressed his models in Italian costume, as here.
The painting is in the Art Institute of Chicago.

steps.title: LADY READING THE LETTERS OF HELOISE AND ABELARD, c. 1780
steps.text: Painted in Paris by Auguste Bernard, called d'Agescy, early in his career. Oil on canvas, 81 by 65 centimetres.

steps.title: LOST IN THOUGHT
steps.text: A young woman leans back, eyes up, lost in a daydream. She has just been reading.

steps.title: THE LETTERS
steps.text: The book in her hand is the letters of Heloise and Abelard: two real lovers of the 1100s. Abelard was a famous teacher in Paris and Heloise his brilliant pupil; their love ended in tragedy, and their letters were read for centuries.

steps.title: THE TABLE
steps.text: On the table beside her: a letter, a sheet of music, a string of pearls and a book of poetry. Each hints at a life of leisure and a heart ready for love.

steps.title: SILK AND SKIN
steps.text: The pink silk, white gown and soft light come from older masters: Rubens and Le Brun, and the Paris painter of feeling, Greuze.

steps.title: A CAREER CUT SHORT
steps.text:
D'Agescy studied in Italy. When he came back to Paris, the French Revolution and a new taste for the plainer Neoclassical style left him little work.
The painting is in the Art Institute of Chicago.

steps.title: THE BEDROOM, 1889
steps.text: Vincent van Gogh's bedroom in his "Yellow House" in Arles, in the south of France. He painted it three times; this is the second, made in September 1889.

steps.title: THE COLOURS
steps.text: He wrote to his brother Theo that he had painted "the walls pale lilac, the floor in a broken and faded red, the chairs and the bed chrome yellow, the pillows and the sheet very pale lemon green, the bedspread blood-red, the dressing table orange, the washbasin blue, the window green."

steps.title: THE BED
steps.text: The big wooden bed fills the right of the room, its red cover the hottest colour in the picture.

steps.title: THE WINDOW
steps.text: The green window is half open on the south of France.

steps.title: THE PICTURES
steps.text: Over the bed hang two portraits and other little pictures; on the pegs, his clothes and his hat.

steps.title: A RESTFUL ROOM
steps.text:
The lines rush into the distance and the paint is thick and broken, but Van Gogh meant the picture to be calm and restful. He made a third, smaller version as a gift for his mother and sister.
This one is in the Art Institute of Chicago.

steps.title: LANDSCAPE WITH CHARON CROSSING THE STYX
steps.text:
Joachim Patinir painted this in Antwerp, around 1520 to 1524. It hangs in the Prado in Madrid.
It is small, about 64 by 103 centimetres, and visitors are often surprised by it. One wrote that it is small, "but boy I wasn't ready for that blue."

steps.title: CHARON AND HIS PASSENGER
steps.text:
In the middle of the river is Charon, the ferryman of the dead from Greek myth, rowing a small boat. His passenger is a naked soul, a person who has just died.
The river is the Styx. Everything else in the painting is the choice that soul has to make.

steps.title: THE WAY TO PARADISE
steps.text:
On the left bank is paradise: green meadows, clear streams, a crystal fountain and angels walking with souls.
But look at the shore nearest the boat. The way in is narrow, through a thicket, and hard to see.

steps.title: THE WAY TO HELL
steps.text:
On the right bank the trees are gentle and the shore is open, an easy, pleasant landing. It leads straight to the gate of hell, guarded by the three-headed dog Cerberus.
Behind it the sky burns red and the buildings are on fire.

steps.title: WHERE IS THE SOUL LOOKING?
steps.text:
The soul in the boat turns towards hell, towards the easy way.
Patinir is showing a Christian idea from the Gospel of Matthew: the gate to life is narrow and few find it; the road to destruction is wide.

steps.title: THE FIRST LANDSCAPE PAINTER
steps.text:
The tiny figures are almost an excuse. Patinir made the world itself the subject: a high horizon, far blue hills, a river running into the distance.
The German artist Albrecht Dürer, who met him in Antwerp in 1521, called him "the good landscape painter". He is often named as the first painter of landscapes.

steps.title: THE BLUE
steps.text:
The far distance turns blue and pale. Painters call this aerial perspective: air makes faraway things look bluer and fainter.
Patinir pushed it further than anyone before him. The blue of the river and the hills is what people remember when they leave.

steps.title: THE DOG, 1819–23
steps.text:
Francisco de Goya painted this between 1819 and 1823, straight onto the plaster wall of his house outside Madrid. It is now in the Prado.
One visitor said: "Saw Goya's Dog in person and I could barely breathe. Devastating."

steps.title: THE HEAD
steps.text:
Near the bottom, a dog's head looks up from behind a dark slope. That is all we see of it.
Is it sinking in sand, drowning, hiding? Its body is gone. Its eyes are open, looking up.

steps.title: THE EMPTY SPACE
steps.text:
Almost all the rest is empty: a huge field of ochre and grey, with no horizon, no sky you can name.
No painting before it left so much space empty. It looks forward to abstract painting a hundred years later.

steps.title: THE SLOPE
steps.text:
The dark brown shape rising from left to right could be a hill, a wave of earth, or mud.
The dog is too small for the world around it, and alone.

steps.title: THE SHADOW AT THE TOP
steps.text:
Look at the upper right. There is a faint darker shape there. Some think the dog was once looking up at something painted there, a rock or birds, that was lost when the murals were moved.
No one is sure what was intended.

steps.title: THE BLACK PAINTINGS
steps.text:
The Dog is one of fourteen murals Goya painted on the walls of his house, the Quinta del Sordo, the 'Deaf Man's Villa'. He was over seventy, deaf, and had lived through war and illness.
They were never meant to be seen. Today they are called the Black Paintings. Saturn Devouring His Son is one of them.

steps.title: OFF THE WALLS
steps.text:
Around 1874 the paintings were peeled off the walls and moved onto canvas, and they were given to the Prado in 1881.
The name 'The Dog' was given later. Goya himself left no titles and no explanation.

steps.title: SUPPER AT EMMAUS, 1601
steps.text:
Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio painted this in Rome in 1601. It hangs in the National Gallery, London.
The figures are life-size, and they seem to lean right out of the picture into your space.

steps.title: THE STORY
steps.text:
In the Gospel of Luke, two of Jesus's followers walk to the village of Emmaus on the day of the Resurrection. A stranger joins them on the road and they invite him to supper.
When he blesses and breaks the bread, they suddenly recognise him: it is Jesus, risen from the dead. Then he vanishes.

steps.title: CHRIST WITHOUT A BEARD
steps.text:
In the centre Christ raises his hand in blessing. He is young, round-faced and beardless, not the bearded Jesus everyone knew.
Luke says the disciples did not recognise him at first. Caravaggio makes sure we nearly don't either.

steps.title: THE ARMS FLUNG WIDE
steps.text:
On the right, a disciple flings his arms out in shock, one hand reaching towards us and the other back into the dark.
His arms make the shape of the cross. The scallop shell on his coat is the badge of a pilgrim.

steps.title: THE CHAIR
steps.text:
On the left, the other disciple grips his chair, about to jump up. His elbow pokes out at us, and his jacket is torn at the elbow.
These are poor working men, painted from real people in the streets of Rome.

steps.title: THE BASKET ON THE EDGE
steps.text:
The fruit basket hangs over the edge of the table, about to fall into our space. Its shadow falls on the cloth.
Look closely at the fruit: some of it is going bad. Caravaggio painted still life as carefully as faces.

steps.title: THE INNKEEPER
steps.text:
The innkeeper stands with his cap on, puzzled. He sees only a guest, not a miracle.
Christ has no halo. The only sign of something holy is the light on his face, and the innkeeper's shadow on the wall behind him.

steps.title: LIGHT AND DARK
steps.text:
The light falls hard from the upper left, and everything else sinks into black. Painters call this chiaroscuro, light-dark; Caravaggio pushed it so far it got its own name, tenebrism.
Five years later he killed a man in a fight and fled Rome. He died in 1610, at 38.

steps.title: THE ENTOMBMENT, c. 1500–01
steps.text:
Michelangelo Buonarroti painted this in Rome around 1500 to 1501, when he was about 25, just after he carved the Pietà in St Peter's. It hangs in the National Gallery, London.
It is unfinished. It shows how he built a painting, layer by layer.

steps.title: THE BODY OF CHRIST
steps.text:
In the centre, the dead Christ is carried towards his tomb, held up by a strip of linen under his arms.
His body is painted like a statue: pale, smooth, heroic, more like carved marble than flesh. Michelangelo always thought of himself first as a sculptor.

steps.title: THE MAN IN RED
steps.text:
On the left, a young man in a red robe leans back, straining to hold the weight. He is probably John the Evangelist.
His pose twists, his feet braced on the step. You can feel how heavy the body is.

steps.title: THE WOMAN IN GREEN
steps.text:
On the right a woman, one of the followers of Jesus, helps with the other end of the cloth, turning to look back.
Notice how the three figures make an arch around the body, like a doorway.

steps.title: THE KNEELING WOMAN
steps.text:
In the lower left corner, a woman kneels. Her hands and the cloth by her are only sketched in.
She is probably Mary Magdalene, looking at the crown of thorns and the nails, which were never painted.

steps.title: THE EMPTY CORNER
steps.text:
The lower right is bare: just the brownish ground layer, with a figure only outlined.
This was probably meant for Mary, his mother. Michelangelo may have been waiting for expensive ultramarine blue for her robe, the colour always used for Mary. It never came: he left Rome for Florence in 1501 to carve the David.

steps.title: WHY NOT THE SISTINE CHAPEL?
steps.text:
Michelangelo's great paintings, the Sistine Chapel ceiling and The Last Judgment, are in the Vatican, on walls you cannot move.
This museum shows one of the very few paintings on panel by him that survive, in London.

steps.title: THE GARDEN OF EARTHLY DELIGHTS
steps.text:
Hieronymus Bosch painted this triptych, three hinged panels, in the Netherlands sometime between 1490 and 1510. It hangs in the Prado in Madrid.
Open, it is about 2.2 by 3.9 metres. People say you can spend an hour in front of it and still find new things.

steps.title: LEFT: EDEN
steps.text:
The left panel is the Garden of Eden. God, in pink, presents Eve to a just-woken Adam.
But look around them: a cat walks off with a mouse, strange animals eat one another, and an owl, a bird of darkness, peers out of the fountain. Trouble is already in paradise.

steps.title: MIDDLE: THE GARDEN
steps.text:
The big middle panel is crowded with hundreds of naked people playing, riding animals, swimming, picking giant fruit.
It looks like a party. Most scholars read it as a warning: the world given over to pleasure and lust, everyone too busy to notice where it is going.

steps.title: THE RIDERS
steps.text:
Round a pool a parade of men ride horses, camels, pigs and griffins, circling a pool of women.
Giant strawberries, cherries and birds are everywhere. Fruit, in the Dutch sayings of the time, stood for pleasures that do not last.

steps.title: STRANGE THINGS
steps.text:
Zoom in: lovers inside a glass bubble, people in a mussel shell, a man carrying a giant fruit, birds feeding people berries.
No one fully understands it. Bosch left no writing about it.

steps.title: RIGHT: HELL
steps.text:
The right panel is hell, dark and burning. Musical instruments become instruments of torture: a man stretched on a harp, another with music written on his backside.
A bird-headed monster on a chair eats people and drops them through a hole.

steps.title: THE TREE MAN
steps.text:
In the middle of hell stands the Tree Man: a body like a cracked eggshell on legs like tree trunks, with a face that turns to look at you.
It may be Bosch's own face.

steps.title: THE OUTSIDE
steps.text:
When the wings are closed, they show the world on the third day of creation, in grey: a clear globe holding the flat earth, with God tiny at the top.
Philip II of Spain loved Bosch and bought it; it has been in Spain since 1593.

steps.title: THE GHENT ALTARPIECE, 1432
steps.text:
Hubert and Jan van Eyck made this altarpiece for St Bavo's Cathedral in Ghent, Belgium, where it still stands. An inscription says Hubert began it and Jan finished it in 1432.
Open, it is twelve panels of oak, about 3.5 by 4.6 metres. It is one of the most stolen artworks in history.

steps.title: THE ADORATION OF THE MYSTIC LAMB
steps.text:
The great lower panel gives the altarpiece its name. In a meadow full of flowers, crowds of saints, prophets, popes, martyrs and pilgrims come from every side to worship a lamb on an altar.
The lamb stands for Christ, who in Christian belief was sacrificed like a lamb.

steps.title: THE LAMB AND THE FOUNTAIN
steps.text:
Blood pours from the lamb's chest into a golden chalice. Below, the Fountain of Life flows towards the viewer.
In the 1500s someone painted over the lamb's face. When restorers removed that paint in 2019 the original came back: a strangely human face with eyes that look straight at you. The internet was not ready.

steps.title: GOD ENTHRONED
steps.text:
At the top centre sits a figure in red with a jewelled crown at his feet, God or Christ as king.
Zoom in on the jewels and the embroidered hems. Each pearl has its own highlight and shadow.

steps.title: MARY, READING
steps.text:
To the left of God sits the Virgin Mary, crowned, reading a book. On the right is John the Baptist.
The van Eycks did not invent oil paint, but they mastered it. Thin transparent layers, called glazes, give the robes a glow no one had seen before.

steps.title: ADAM
steps.text:
On the far left stands Adam, the first man, almost life-size and fully naked: among the first nudes this real in northern European art.
He stands in a niche high above you, and his right foot seems to step out of it towards you.

steps.title: EVE
steps.text:
Eve faces him from the far right, holding a fruit. Above them, small grey scenes show their sons Cain and Abel and the first murder.
The two were so shocking to later viewers that in the 1800s they were swapped for copies wearing clothes.

steps.title: THE ANGEL MUSICIANS
steps.text:
On this side angels play an organ, a harp and a viol; on the other side angels sing.
Look at the singers' faces. You can almost tell which part each one is singing from how wide their mouths are open.

steps.title: THE STOLEN PANEL
steps.text:
In 1934 the lower-left panel, the Just Judges, was stolen. A ransom note came; it was never found. What you see there is a copy made in 1945.
The whole altarpiece was also taken by Napoleon's armies and by the Nazis, who hid it in a salt mine in Austria, where the Allied 'Monuments Men' found it in 1945.

steps.title: THE BODY OF THE DEAD CHRIST IN THE TOMB, 1520–22
steps.text:
Hans Holbein the Younger painted this in Basel, Switzerland, around 1520 to 1522, when he was in his early twenties. It hangs in the Kunstmuseum Basel.
It is only 30.5 centimetres high but two metres long: life-size, the length of a man lying down.

steps.title: A BOX FOR A BODY
steps.text:
Christ lies alone in a narrow stone tomb, seen from the side, as if the lid has been lifted. There are no angels, no mourners, no light from heaven.
The painting is the shape of the tomb itself. Standing in front of it you are looking into a coffin.

steps.title: THE FACE
steps.text:
His eyes are half open and rolled back, his mouth hangs open. The skin around the face has started to turn grey-green.
This is not a sleeping saint. It is a dead man, three days in the tomb, and Holbein does not look away.

steps.title: THE WOUNDS
steps.text:
The wound in his side and the wounds in his hand and feet are painted plainly, like a doctor's record.
Holbein may have painted from a real corpse; one story says it was a body pulled from the Rhine.

steps.title: THE HAND
steps.text:
His right hand lies at his side, the middle finger stretched out, almost touching the edge of the frame, the wound dark and open.
It reaches towards us, out of the tomb.

steps.title: THE FEET
steps.text:
His feet break past the line of the stone, almost out of the box. His hair spills over the edge at the other end.
The body is too long for the space it is in, which makes the tomb feel even tighter.

steps.title: DOSTOEVSKY
steps.text:
In 1867 the Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky stood in front of it in Basel for so long that his wife feared he was having an epileptic fit.
In his novel The Idiot a character says a man could lose his faith from looking at this painting. Above it, in Latin, the frame reads: Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.

steps.title: THE KISS, 1907–08
steps.text:
Gustav Klimt painted this in Vienna in 1907 and 1908. It hangs in the Belvedere in Vienna.
It is square, 180 by 180 centimetres, and covered in real gold leaf. People often say they did not expect it to glow like it does.

steps.title: THE GOLDEN PERIOD
steps.text:
Klimt's father was a gold engraver. In 1903 Klimt saw the golden Byzantine mosaics in the churches of Ravenna, in Italy, and they changed his work.
This is the high point of what is called his Golden Period. The Austrian state bought it before it was even finished.

steps.title: THE FACES
steps.text:
The man bends his head down to kiss the woman's cheek. Her eyes are closed, her face turned up towards us.
We never see his face. Whether she is giving in to him or holding back is left for you to decide.

steps.title: HIS ROBE
steps.text: His robe is covered in black, white and silver rectangles, hard and upright.

steps.title: HER DRESS
steps.text:
Hers is full of circles and flowers in red, blue and violet.
Square for the man, round for the woman: two patterns that meet and melt into one golden shape.

steps.title: HER FEET AND THE EDGE
steps.text:
They kneel at the very edge of a flowery meadow. Her bare feet curl over the edge, and vines trail from her ankles into nothing.
One more step and they would fall. The love is held at the edge of a drop.

steps.title: THE GOLD BACKGROUND
steps.text:
The background is not a place. It is a shimmering field of gold and bronze, scattered with flecks like stars or dust.
It takes the couple out of time, the way a gold background lifts a saint out of the world in an old icon.

steps.title: THE COUPLE
steps.text:
No one knows for certain who posed. Many think the woman is Emilie Flöge, a fashion designer and Klimt's lifelong companion, and the man Klimt himself.
Klimt died in 1918. The Kiss is now one of the best-known paintings in the world.

steps.title: WATER LILIES (AGAPANTHUS), c. 1915–26
steps.text:
Claude Monet painted this in his garden at Giverny, in France, late in his life. It hangs in the Cleveland Museum of Art.
It is about two metres high and over four metres wide. Monet's water lilies are the paintings people say you have to stand in front of to understand.

steps.title: THE POND
steps.text:
In 1893 Monet bought land next to his house, dug a pond, and planted it with water lilies. He built a Japanese bridge over it.
For his last thirty years he painted almost nothing else: about 250 paintings of the pond.

steps.title: LILY PADS
steps.text:
Across the top float clusters of lily pads, green and yellow, with pink touches where the flowers open.
There is no shore, no horizon and no sky. You are looking straight down into the water.

steps.title: THE SKY IN THE WATER
steps.text:
The blues and violets are the sky and clouds reflected in the pond.
Monet paints three layers at once: the surface with its lilies, the reflection of the sky on it, and the plants under the water.

steps.title: THE REEDS
steps.text:
At the bottom, long strokes of green rise like grasses and reeds growing at the water's edge, or under the surface.
Up close it is only paint, scraped and dragged. Step back and it becomes water.

steps.title: THE FLOWERS
steps.text:
Small red and yellow blooms glow in the lower right.
The title's other flower, agapanthus, was once on this canvas too: Monet painted the tall blue flowers along the bank and later painted them out.

steps.title: OLD AND NEARLY BLIND
steps.text:
Monet was in his seventies and losing his sight to cataracts while he painted these. Colours went muddy and brown to him.
This canvas is one part of a huge three-part work. The other two parts are in Saint Louis and Kansas City. Monet's largest water lilies fill two oval rooms in the Musée de l'Orangerie in Paris.

steps.title: MASSACRE OF THE INNOCENTS, c. 1611–12
steps.text:
Peter Paul Rubens painted this in Antwerp around 1611 to 1612, soon after he came home from eight years in Italy. It hangs in the Art Gallery of Ontario in Toronto.
It is a terrible subject, and people who see it say it stays with them.

steps.title: THE STORY
steps.text:
In the Gospel of Matthew, King Herod hears that a king of the Jews has been born in Bethlehem. Afraid, he orders his soldiers to kill every boy there under two years old.
Rubens shows the moment the soldiers reach the mothers.

steps.title: THE SOLDIER WITH THE CHILD
steps.text:
At the top right a huge, muscled soldier lifts a baby by its legs over his head, about to throw it to the ground.
Rubens had studied ancient Roman statues in Italy, and these bodies are built like them: twisting, straining, full of force.

steps.title: THE MOTHERS FIGHT BACK
steps.text:
In the centre the mothers do not just weep. They claw at the soldiers' faces, pull their hair, and grab their arms.
One woman digs her nails into a soldier's face while he pulls her down.

steps.title: THE RED CLOTH
steps.text:
A woman in a blazing red dress sweeps across the bottom of the scene, her child torn from her.
The red leads your eye down to the floor, where the worst of it lies.

steps.title: THE FLOOR
steps.text:
Along the ground lie the dead babies, pale and soft, painted with great tenderness. A little blood runs between the stones.
Rubens makes them beautiful, which makes it harder to look at.

steps.title: THE CALM CITY
steps.text:
Behind it all, in the upper left, a calm city of temples and columns under a blue sky. Tiny figures there are still running.
The world goes on while this happens.

steps.title: LOST AND FOUND
steps.text:
For centuries the painting was thought to be by one of Rubens's pupils. In 2002 it was recognised as his own work and sold at auction for £49.5 million, then the highest price ever paid for an Old Master.
The buyer, the Canadian Ken Thomson, gave it to the Art Gallery of Ontario.

steps.title: LAS MENINAS, 1656
steps.text:
Diego Velázquez painted this in Madrid in 1656, as court painter to King Philip IV of Spain. It hangs in the Prado.
It is over three metres tall. Painters and writers have argued about it for 350 years; the painter Luca Giordano called it "the theology of painting".

steps.title: THE PRINCESS
steps.text:
In the middle, lit up, stands the five-year-old Infanta Margarita Teresa, the king's daughter, in a wide silver dress.
The Spanish title means 'the ladies-in-waiting': the two young women at her side, who are tending to her.

steps.title: THE PAINTER
steps.text:
On the left Velázquez paints himself at a huge canvas, brush in hand, looking out at us.
We cannot see what he is painting. On his chest is the red cross of the Order of Santiago, a high honour. It was added after he received it in 1659, three years after the picture was done, probably by order of the king.

steps.title: THE MIRROR
steps.text:
On the back wall hangs a mirror. In it are two faces: King Philip IV and Queen Mariana.
So they are standing where you are standing. Everyone in the room is looking at them, which means at you. The picture turns you into the king.

steps.title: THE MAN IN THE DOORWAY
steps.text:
At the back, a man stands on the stairs in an open door, light behind him: José Nieto, the queen's chamberlain.
He could be coming or going. He gives the room its depth, pulling your eye all the way through it.

steps.title: THE DWARFS AND THE DOG
steps.text:
On the right are two court dwarfs, Mari Bárbola and Nicolasito Pertusato, who is resting his foot on a big sleepy mastiff.
Velázquez paints them with the same seriousness and dignity as the princess.

steps.title: THE BRUSHWORK
steps.text:
Zoom in on the princess's dress or hair. Close up it falls apart into loose dabs and smears of paint. From a distance it becomes silk and light.
Two hundred years later Édouard Manet saw it in Madrid and called Velázquez "the painter of painters".

steps.title: PICASSO'S MENINAS
steps.text:
In 1957 Pablo Picasso shut himself away and painted 58 versions of Las Meninas.
It hangs in the Prado's main hall today and is often called the greatest painting in the museum.

steps.title: THE NIGHT WATCH, 1642
steps.text:
Rembrandt van Rijn finished this in Amsterdam in 1642. It hangs in its own hall in the Rijksmuseum.
It is huge, about 3.8 by 4.5 metres, and the figures are life-size. It was once even bigger: in 1715 strips were cut off all four sides to fit it on a wall in the town hall.

steps.title: NOT A NIGHT
steps.text:
It is not a night scene. Its real title is Militia Company of District II under the Command of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq.
Over centuries its varnish darkened so much that people thought it was set at night, and the nickname stuck. It is a daytime scene.

steps.title: THE CAPTAIN
steps.text:
In the centre, in black with a red sash, Captain Frans Banninck Cocq strides towards us, his hand reaching out as he gives the order to march.
Look at his hand: its shadow falls across his lieutenant's yellow coat.

steps.title: THE LIEUTENANT
steps.text:
Beside him in pale yellow is Lieutenant Willem van Ruytenburch. The pale coat and the black one set each other off.
Zoom in on his coat: it is embroidered with the lion of Amsterdam, and his spear seems to poke out of the picture.

steps.title: THE GIRL IN GOLD
steps.text:
Behind them, in a pool of light, is a strange small girl in gold with a dead chicken hanging from her belt.
The chicken's claws are the emblem of the militia company, the arquebusiers. She is a living mascot.

steps.title: MOVEMENT
steps.text:
Group portraits of militia companies usually lined everyone up in rows, like a team photo.
Rembrandt shows them in action instead: loading guns, raising flags, a dog barking, a drummer beating. The company is just starting to march out.

steps.title: THE DRUMMER
steps.text:
On the right a drummer beats his drum, and a dog barks at him underneath.
You can almost hear it.

steps.title: OPERATION NIGHT WATCH
steps.text:
The eighteen men named on the shield by the arch each paid to be in it. The painting has been attacked three times, cut with knives in 1911 and 1975 and sprayed with acid in 1990, and it was hidden in a cave during the Second World War.
Since 2019 it has been studied and restored in a glass room in the museum, in front of visitors.

steps.title: GIRL WITH A PEARL EARRING, c. 1665
steps.text:
Johannes Vermeer painted this in Delft around 1665. It hangs in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.
It is only 44.5 by 39 centimetres. People who have seen it are often surprised how small it is, and how alive.

steps.title: NOT A PORTRAIT
steps.text:
She is not a known person. This is a tronie, the Dutch word for a study of a face, an expression or a costume, sold as a picture in itself.
No one knows who sat for it. The novel and film about a maid in Vermeer's house are invented.

steps.title: THE TURBAN
steps.text:
The blue of her turban is ultramarine, made from ground lapis lazuli, a stone mined in Afghanistan. It cost more than gold.
Vermeer used it even though he was often in debt. The turban is exotic dress, not something a Dutch girl wore.

steps.title: THE PEARL
steps.text:
Zoom in on the pearl. It has no outline and no hook to hang from the ear. It is two strokes: a bright highlight at the top and a soft reflection of her white collar at the bottom.
It is so big that it may not be a pearl at all, but polished glass or tin.

steps.title: THE EYES AND MOUTH
steps.text:
She turns over her shoulder as if you just spoke to her. Her lips are parted and wet, with a tiny white highlight.
A study of the painting in 2018 found she once had eyelashes, now gone.

steps.title: THE DARK BACKGROUND
steps.text:
The background looks black and flat. It was once a deep green curtain, painted with a glaze that has faded over 350 years.
Without the curtain she seems to float, closer than anyone in a painting should be.

steps.title: HOW HE PAINTED
steps.text:
Vermeer painted slowly, maybe three pictures a year, and fewer than 40 survive.
He died in 1675, poor, and was nearly forgotten for two hundred years. This painting sold at auction in 1881 for two guilders and thirty cents.

steps.title: THE RAFT OF THE MEDUSA, 1818–19
steps.text:
Théodore Géricault painted this in Paris when he was 27. It hangs in the Louvre.
It is enormous: about 4.9 by 7.2 metres, the figures at the front larger than life. One visitor said it was "the only painting I remember from the Louvre... like you could have stepped into it."

steps.title: WHAT HAPPENED
steps.text:
In July 1816 the French navy frigate Méduse ran aground off the coast of West Africa. Its captain was a nobleman with almost no time at sea, given the post for his politics.
There were not enough lifeboats. About 147 people were put on a raft that was meant to be towed. The ropes were cut, and the raft was left to drift.

steps.title: THE SIGNAL
steps.text:
At the top right a man is held up by the others, waving a cloth at a ship on the horizon.
On the thirteenth day the brig Argus came. Only fifteen of the 147 were still alive. Géricault chose the moment of hope, when they do not yet know if they will be seen.

steps.title: THE SHIP
steps.text:
Look for the tiny ship on the horizon, just right of the waving cloth. It is almost nothing, a speck.
The whole picture strains towards it.

steps.title: THE FATHER
steps.text:
On the left an older man sits holding a dead young man across his lap, turned away from the hope.
On the raft the survivors had fought, starved, and some had eaten the dead. Géricault leaves that out but shows despair beside hope.

steps.title: THE PYRAMID
steps.text:
The bodies are built into two pyramids: one up the mast and the sail on the left, a bigger one rising from the dead at the front to the man waving at the top right.
Your eye climbs from death at the bottom to hope at the top.

steps.title: HOW HE MADE IT
steps.text:
Géricault interviewed two survivors and had a model of the raft built. He studied the dead and dying in hospitals and kept body parts in his studio to paint from.
It caused a scandal at the Salon of 1819: a real disaster and a government's failure, painted at the size of a history painting meant for kings and gods.

steps.title: THE STARRY NIGHT, JUNE 1889
steps.text:
Vincent van Gogh painted this in June 1889 at the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in Saint-Rémy, in the south of France. He had admitted himself there after a breakdown.
It hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. It is 74 by 92 centimetres, smaller than most people expect.

steps.title: THE MOON
steps.text:
Top right is a crescent moon wrapped in a huge glowing halo, painted as one bright orange and yellow shape.
The moon is glowing like a sun. Nothing in the sky is painted the way it really looks.

steps.title: THE SWIRL
steps.text:
Across the middle of the sky rolls a great spiral, like a wave or a wind you can see.
People have compared it to drawings of spiral galaxies and to the way turbulent air and water move.

steps.title: THE STARS
steps.text:
Eleven stars, each with rings of light around it.
Van Gogh wrote to his brother Theo that the countryside at night was "even more richly coloured than the day", and that the sight of the stars always made him dream.
The bright one by the cypress is likely Venus, the morning star, which shone just before dawn that month.

steps.title: THE CYPRESS
steps.text:
In front rises a dark cypress tree, like a flame, tying the ground to the sky.
Cypresses grow in cemeteries in the south of France and were linked with death. Van Gogh also wrote that they were "beautiful as an Egyptian obelisk".

steps.title: THE VILLAGE
steps.text:
Below sits a quiet village under the hills, its windows lit, the church spire pointing up.
His window had bars and looked over fields, not a village. He painted the view partly from memory and imagination, and the spire looks more Dutch than French, like the churches of his childhood.

steps.title: THE BRUSHSTROKES
steps.text:
Zoom in: the paint is thick, laid down in short curved strokes that all flow in one direction, like iron filings around a magnet.
You can follow the movement of his hand across the whole sky.

steps.title: A FAILURE, HE THOUGHT
steps.text:
Van Gogh was not happy with it. He called it a failure in a letter to Theo.
He died a year later, in July 1890. The painting went to MoMA in 1941 and is now among the most famous pictures in the world.

steps.title: THE FIGHTING TEMERAIRE, 1839
steps.text:
J. M. W. Turner painted this in 1839. Its full title is The Fighting Temeraire, tugged to her last berth to be broken up, 1838. It hangs in the National Gallery, London.
One visitor wrote that it is "the only painting that has ever brought me to tears". In 2005 the British public voted it the greatest painting in Britain.

steps.title: THE OLD WARSHIP
steps.text:
The ghostly ship on the left is HMS Temeraire, a 98-gun warship. In 1805 she fought at the Battle of Trafalgar, where the British fleet beat the French and Spanish and Admiral Nelson was killed.
Turner paints her pale gold and white, almost like a spirit.

steps.title: THE TUG
steps.text:
Pulling her is a small, dark steam tug, its tall funnel pouring smoke and fire.
The old sailing world is being towed away by the new world of steam and industry. The tug is ugly next to her, and it is in charge.

steps.title: THE MASTS
steps.text:
In real life her masts and sails had already been taken off before this journey.
Turner gives her back her tall masts. He was not painting a report, he was painting a farewell.

steps.title: THE SUNSET
steps.text:
On the right the sun goes down in a blaze of orange, red and yellow, laid on thickly with a palette knife.
A setting sun for a ship going to her death, and for an age that was ending. The pale moon rises on the left over the ship.

steps.title: THE BUOY
steps.text:
Low on the right, a dark buoy floats in the water, a small black mark that steadies all that light.
Up close the sky is almost abstract: smears and scrapes of paint. Step back and it becomes air and fire.

steps.title: TURNER'S DARLING
steps.text:
Turner called it his "darling". He refused every offer to buy it and left it to the nation when he died in 1851.
Since 2020 it has been on the Bank of England's twenty-pound note, with Turner's self-portrait.

steps.title: VENUS AND MARS, c. 1485
steps.text:
Sandro Botticelli painted this in Florence around 1485, a few years before The Birth of Venus. It hangs in the National Gallery, London.
It is long and low, about 69 by 173 centimetres, the shape of a panel set into a bed's headboard or a chest, probably made for a wedding.

steps.title: VENUS, AWAKE
steps.text:
On the left lies Venus, goddess of love, fully dressed in a white gown edged with gold, sitting up and watching.
She looks calm and in control. Her face is the same type Botticelli gives Venus in The Birth of Venus.

steps.title: MARS, ASLEEP
steps.text:
On the right sprawls Mars, god of war, naked and in a deep sleep, his head thrown back and his mouth open.
The god of war has been disarmed by love. The message is old and simple: love conquers war.

steps.title: THE LITTLE SATYRS
steps.text:
Baby satyrs, half child and half goat, play with his weapons: one wears his huge helmet, another carries his lance, another crawls through his armour.
One blows a conch shell right into his ear. He does not wake.

steps.title: THE WASPS
steps.text:
Look at the top right corner, by Mars's head: a swarm of wasps flies out of a tree.
In Italian a wasp is a vespa. This may be a joke on the Vespucci, a Florentine family whose coat of arms showed wasps; they may have ordered the painting.

steps.title: THE DETAIL
steps.text:
Zoom in on the folds of Venus's dress, the gold edging, the curls of her hair.
Botticelli drew with a fine, flowing line, and painted in egg tempera and oil on wood, which keeps the colours sharp and clear.

steps.title: WHY NOT THE BIRTH OF VENUS?
steps.text:
The Birth of Venus hangs in the Uffizi in Florence. Italy's state museums control how pictures of their works are used, so this museum shows Botticelli's Venus from London instead.
The two were painted in the same years by the same hand.

steps.title: WANDERER ABOVE THE SEA OF FOG
steps.text:
Caspar David Friedrich, the German Romantic painter, made this around 1818. It hangs in the Hamburger Kunsthalle in Hamburg.
It is about 95 by 75 centimetres, and it has become the picture of the whole Romantic age.

steps.title: THE MAN FROM BEHIND
steps.text:
A man in a dark green coat stands on a rock with a walking stick, his back to us. We never see his face.
Painters call this a Rückenfigur, a figure seen from behind. We look over his shoulder, so we stand where he stands and feel what he feels.

steps.title: THE SEA OF FOG
steps.text:
Below him the valleys are drowned in fog. Only the tops of rocks and trees stick out like islands.
The place is real: the sandstone mountains of Saxon Switzerland, near Dresden. Friedrich sketched the rocks on walks and put them together in the studio. The view as a whole never existed.

steps.title: THE FAR MOUNTAINS
steps.text:
Far away, mountains rise out of the haze and fade into the sky.
The Romantics called this feeling the sublime: beauty mixed with awe, even fear, at something far bigger than you.

steps.title: THE DARK ROCK
steps.text:
The rock he stands on is nearly black, solid and heavy, against the pale world beyond. There is no middle ground between him and the distance.
One step and he would be part of it.

steps.title: WHO IS HE?
steps.text:
No one knows. He may be Friedrich himself, or a fallen soldier of the wars against Napoleon; he wears an old German style of dress that patriots wore then.
After Friedrich died in 1840 he was almost forgotten. He was rediscovered around 1900, and today this is one of the most copied images in the world.
